desc:
There are n people labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry friendships[i] = [a, b] makes a and b friends. A friend circle is a maximal group of people connected by chains of friendships (a person without friends is a circle of one).

Each entry rivalries[j] = [x, y] says that x and y are rivals. A circle is peaceful if no two members of it are rivals. Rivals who sit in different circles do not matter. Return the number of peaceful circles.

n = 6, friendships = [[0,1],[1,2],[3,4]], rivalries = [[0,2],[2,5]]

result = 2     (circle {0,1,2} contains rivals 0 and 2; {3,4} and {5} are peaceful)
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b, x, y < n, a ≠ b and x ≠ y
No pair appears twice within friendships, none twice within rivalries, and no pair is in both lists
hints: First work out which circle every person is in; the rivalries only matter in comparison with that.
A rivalry [x, y] ruins a circle exactly when x and y belong to the same circle. A rivalry between two different circles ruins nothing.
Union all friendships. Then for each rivalry, if find(x) == find(y), mark that root as unpeaceful. The answer is the number of distinct roots minus the number of marked roots.
editorial: Build the circles with union-find over the friendships. Then scan the rivalries: for each pair, compare the two roots. If they are equal, the circle with that root contains two rivals, so add the root to a set of spoiled circles. Rivalries across different circles are ignored.

The number of circles equals the number of distinct roots over all n people (equivalently n minus the number of successful unions). The answer is that number minus the size of the spoiled set. Total time is O((n + m + k) · α(n)) for m friendships and k rivalries.
